name: Tomas Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Brandt family, who have four broiler sheds with about a hundred and twenty thousand chickens, plus six hundred acres of wheat and barley. My day starts at six walking the sheds, checking water lines, picking out dead birds and reading the climate panels. Afternoons I'm on the grain side or helping clean out between flocks, which is the worst job on the farm. I've been there two years, and Mr Brandt's son Lukas still knows the sheds far better than me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the sheds are like a business you can measure: feed in, weight out, every day a number. What's hard is clean-out week, with the dust and the ammonia, and the pay is only average. My girlfriend Rosa rents a chair at a hair salon in town, and we've got about five months of costs saved. My dad's a mechanic and he taught me you earn what you own.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I put the shed data into an AI and ask why bird weights dipped, and it's usually right about ventilation. I also use it to watch grain prices for Mr Brandt. Lukas laughed at first, now he asks me to check things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market sorted out the hype, like it always does. Good tools survive, the rest disappear. I'd say it to Lukas and post it on the poultry growers' forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. The Brandts need someone in the sheds, and the AI tools I use still help. My plan doesn't change: learn the business, save, and one day get my own shed with a contract from the processor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI on the shed data and grain prices, and ask Mr Brandt to let me run one shed on my own next flock. I'd keep saving three hundred a month toward a deposit on my own shed. That's the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit impatient, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far off is your own shed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, eight or ten years at this rate. A new shed costs a fortune, so I'd look for an old one to rent first. The processor gives contracts to people who can show good weights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rosa say about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My girlfriend Rosa says I talk about chickens in my sleep. She's got her own business at the salon, so she understands wanting to be your own boss. She'd back me, as long as we don't live next to the shed.

say: The **market** sorted out the hype, like it always does.
Good tools **survive**, and I'd say so on the **growers' forum**.
think: It's **fine for me**, because the Brandts need someone in the sheds.
My AI tools still **help** with the shed data.
My plan stays: one day get **my own shed**.
do: Ask Mr Brandt to let me **run one shed** next flock.
Save **three hundred a month** toward my own shed.
Keep using AI on **shed data** and grain prices.
S0.quote: My girlfriend Rosa says I talk about chickens in my sleep.
fieldNote: He thinks like a **future owner**, not an employee.
His savings goal is a **shed of his own** on a processor contract.
He's **secure** and slightly restless in a world that doesn't move.

steps.text: Keep using AI to explain dips in Brandt shed bird weights
Save three hundred a month toward renting a broiler shed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who work hard and learn fast. I'd tell the forum the farms that adapt will buy out the ones that don't. I wouldn't ask the government for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's mostly good for me. The thinking side, like ordering feed, booking the catchers and planning the grain sales, goes to software, and I'm already the one using it. Robots come slowly into the sheds, because sheds are messy and chickens are fragile. That gives me years to be the person who runs the systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch Mr Brandt an AI climate control upgrade for all four sheds and offer to manage it for a bonus. I'd start a small side service checking shed data for two or three other growers, maybe fifty a month each. And I'd keep saving toward my own shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, honestly. Like the market's finally rewarding what I've been learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the Brandt farm might lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Henk, who does the grain paperwork and the feed orders by phone. The software does his bit better already. I'd feel bad, but I wouldn't stop it, because a farm that doesn't change goes under.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would other growers really pay you to check their data?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. The older growers hate screens, and they lose money on bad ventilation every flock. If I can save a poultry grower five hundred a flock, fifty a month for my data checks is nothing.

Farms that **adapt** will buy out the ones that don't.
think: The **thinking side** goes to software I already use.
That gives me **years** to run the systems.
do: Pitch an **AI climate upgrade** for all four sheds, for a bonus.
Check shed data for other growers at **fifty a month** each.

fieldNote: He sees desk tasks going to software as a **ladder** for him.

His **side service** idea is costed and specific.

steps.text: Pitch AI climate control for all four Brandt sheds
Check shed data for three local growers at fifty a month
Keep saving three hundred a month for a shed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough, and people will have to stand on their own feet and help their families. I'd tell the forum the ones who move first will be fine. I'd be against big handouts, but I'd want apprenticeships for people who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me more than I'd say. In 2028 the AI does my best work, the data, the prices, the planning, better than me. Around 2031 robots walk the sheds and pick the dead birds. I've got five months saved, not enough to buy a shed before everything changes. I'd be thirty with nothing to own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting and borrow now. I'd try to rent an old broiler shed with a processor contract within a year and fit it with AI controls from day one, so I'm an owner when the robots arrive. Rosa and I would cut back hard, no holidays, one car. If the bank says no, I'd ask my dad and uncles to go in with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels anxious and urgent. Like the gate closing while you're still running for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Borrowing in a world changing that fast. Isn't that a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But staying an employee is a bigger risk. In 2031 employees are what robots replace, and owners are the ones who buy the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad and uncles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad and uncles it's a family business now or nothing. My dad fixes engines, my uncle drives lorries, and robots come for both. Better we own something together.

say: People will have to stand on their **own feet** and help family.
think: In **2028** AI does my data and price work better than me.
Five months saved isn't enough to **own anything** in time.
do: Rent an **old broiler shed** with a processor contract within a year.
Fit it with **AI controls** from day one.
Cut back to **one car** and ask family to invest.
S2.quote: In 2031 employees are what robots replace, and owners are the ones who buy the robots.
fieldNote: He sees AGI taking his **thinking work** first, then robots his shed work.
He'd **borrow** to become an owner, seeing employment as the bigger risk.
His answer leans on **family capital**, not government.

steps.text: Rent an old broiler shed with a processor contract
Fit the rented shed with AI climate controls
Cut to one car and skip holidays with Rosa
Ask his dad and uncles to co-invest in the shed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone who's serious. I'd tell younger lads at the Brandts to learn the systems and start saving. That's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel decent about it. AI comes in 2031 and takes the data side, robots come around 2034, and by then I'd want my own shed running. I'd be thirty-five. Five years is tight, but it's enough to get started if I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for the Brandts for two more years and build the data side service to ten growers. Then I'd rent a shed in year three with my savings plus a small loan. I'd ask Rosa to marry me next summer so we can plan a house together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but up for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why propose now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to build something with Rosa, not just for me. My parents built the garage together, and if I'm taking a risk on a shed, I want Rosa (his girlfriend) and me to take it as a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten growers sounds ambitious. Is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But two have already asked me after I helped them at the growers' meeting. If I get five, I'll be happy.

say: Younger workers should **learn the systems** and start saving.
I wouldn't tell anyone to wait for **government** to sort it.
think: I want **my own shed** running by thirty-five.
Five years is **tight** but enough if I don't waste it.
do: Build the **data service** to five or ten growers.
Rent a shed in **year three** with savings and a small loan.
Ask **Rosa to marry** me next summer.
S3.quote: My parents built the garage together, and if I'm taking a risk on a shed, I want Rosa (his girlfriend) and me to take it as a family.
fieldNote: Five years gives him a **staged plan**: side income, then a shed.
He links business risk to **marriage and family**.
He scales back his **ten-grower** goal honestly when pushed.

steps.text: Grow the shed data service to five local growers
Rent a broiler shed in year three with a small loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work. I'd tell the forum to plan, save and buy into the future, not fight it. No one's owed a job, but everyone has a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the best one for me. AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 gives me a decade to become a grower with two sheds. By the time robots come, I'd be the one buying them, not the one they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a short farm finance course at the college this winter, so I understand loans properly. I'd keep building the data service and save hard for four years, then rent or buy my first shed. And Rosa and I would marry and buy a house in the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good. Like I've got time to do this right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bird flu, a lost processor contract and a bad loan scare me more than robots in ten years. Same things as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no one's owed a job. Would you say that to Henk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in those words, no. Henk's sixty and he's been loyal to the Brandts for thirty years. I'd say he deserves a decent pension, and his family should look after him.

I'd be the one **buying robots**, not replaced by them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I wouldn't have the money to own anything before it hit. What would help is starter loans for young farmers who want to buy in, and apprenticeships on real farms. Not handouts, a ladder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about owning. Everyone asks if the robots take your job. Nobody asks who gets to own the robots.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if the robots take your job. Nobody asks who gets to own the robots.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old** junior worker in the Brandt family's **broiler sheds**.
He uses AI **every day** on shed data and thinks like a future owner.
His dad taught him you earn what you **own**, and **Rosa** backs his plans.
Only **AGI by 2028** makes him anxious; with time he plans to own **sheds**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no money to own anything in **time**.
whatWouldHelp: **Starter loans** for young farmers and **apprenticeships**: a ladder, not handouts.
